content: The duration of breastfeeding was categorized into the following groups: not breastfed at all, breastfed for less than one month, breastfed for one to three months, or breastfed for three months or longer. Taylor (2011): This study was excluded because it was a protocol for a randomized controlled trial (RCT) where one arm involved breastfeeding promotion. Tehranian (2010): This study was excluded as it was a case-control study. Terati (2018): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Thomas (1993): This study was excluded as it was a case-control study where both cases and controls were selected from hospital admissions, making the sample unrepresentative of the general population. Thomsen (2006): This study was excluded because it did not investigate continued breastfeeding. Thorsdottir (2003): This study was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. The duration of exclusive breastfeeding was used as a continuous variable in regression analyses. Thwin (2016): This study was excluded because it analyzed the effects of both prolonged bottle feeding and breastfeeding on dental caries, rather than focusing on breastfeeding alone. Titus-Ernstoff (2001): This study was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Torris (2013): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. The durations used for analysis were less than three months, three to six months, and more than six months. Toschke (2007): This study was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. The reported durations were less than and more than ten months. Tozzi (2012): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as never, three months, 3–5 months, and more than six months. Troisi (1995): This study was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. The analysis focused on exclusive breastfeeding durations of less than and more than six months. Tsvetov (2014): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Tung (2003): This study was excluded because it was a case-control study. The duration of breastfeeding was studied as a continuous variable using logistic regression. Turton (2016): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Tyagi (2008): This study was excluded because data on dental caries was not provided with reference to varying durations of breastfeeding. The data pertained to the DFS index in caries cases. Tympa-Psirropoulou (2005): This study was excluded because it did not study continued breastfeeding. Tympa-Psirropoulou (2008): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations studied were not at all, three months, six months, and more than six months. United Kingdom National Case Control Study Group: This study was excluded because it was a case-control study not nested in a population cohort. Cases were identified from 11 health regions in the United Kingdom. Ursin (2004, 2005): These studies were excluded because they were hospital-based case-control studies. Vasquez (2019): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. It studied the impact of breastfeeding duration of less than seven months and greater than or equal to seven months. Vella (1995): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Not being breastfed was studied as a variable in regression analysis for stunting. Velle-Forbord (2019): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. It estimated the effects of breastfeeding duration (less than three months, 3–6 months, and more than six months) on metabolic health parameters from baseline to follow-up. Victora (1991): This study was excluded because it lacked a control group. The cohort was followed up at three time points, and nutritional status was compared between breastfed and non-breastfed children. However, no comparison was available for children with prolonged versus shorter breastfeeding durations. Virtanen (1991): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Lactation duration data was presented up to nine months. Vogazianos (2007): This study was excluded because the subjects were not healthy; all included subjects had adenoid hypertrophy. Vogelezang (2018): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations analyzed were nine months and six months. Waidyatillake (2016): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Logistic regression was performed for each additional week of breastfeeding's impact on lung function, height, and other outcomes. Waka (1995): This study was excluded because it was a hospital-based case-control study. Wang (1992, 2006, 2016, 2017, 2017a): These studies were excluded because they did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations were categorized into various groups, such as less than four months, 4–6 months, and more than six months. Wegienka (2006): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations used for analysis were never, 0–1 month, 2–3 months, 4–5 months, 6–9 months, and more than ten months. Wen (2014): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Reported durations were less than and more than six months. Wetzig (2000): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations used for analysis were 0–5 months and more than or equal to five months. Weyermann (2006): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations used for analysis were less than three months, 3–6 months, 6–9 months, and more than or equal to nine months. Whaley (2017): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Logistic regression was performed for each month of breastfeeding's impact on obesity. Whitemore (1993): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. It compared breastfed with never breastfed children and used lactation duration as a continuous variable. Wienfield (2020): This study was excluded because the outcome of interest was not relevant. It studied diet quality as the outcome. Wiklund (2012): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Prolonged breastfeeding was defined as more than ten months. Woo (2008): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations were categorized as 54 months or more than four months. Wright (2000, 2001): These studies were excluded because they did not examine continued breastfeeding. Exclusive breastfeeding durations were categorized as never, less than four months, or more than or equal to four months. Wu (1996): This study was excluded because it was a case-control study with cases selected from various institutions. Yang (2018): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Yazdani (2011): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. It analyzed breastfeeding duration as a continuous variable in relation to maternal osteoporosis. Yazici (2011): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Participants were divided into four groups based on breastfeeding duration: never, 1–24 months, 25–60 months, or more than 60 months. Yelverton (2020): This study was excluded because the outcome of interest was not relevant. It studied child eating behavior. Yokoi (2020): This study was excluded because prolonged breastfeeding was defined as more than 18 months and compared with no prolonged breastfeeding. Yonezu (2006): This study was excluded because it lacked a comparison group and only studied children with continued breastfeeding. Yuan (1988): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Cumulative lactation durations used for analysis were 1–36 months, 37–72 months, 73–108 months, and more than 108 months. Yun (2016): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. It studied breastfeeding durations of less than and more than 24 months. Zhang (2003, 2004a, 2017): These studies were excluded because they did not examine continued breastfeeding. Exclusive breastfeeding durations of less than and more than six months were studied. Zhao (2020): This study was excluded because data was not presented for breastfeeding beyond 12 months. Breastfeeding durations were categorized into three groups for analysis: less than three months, 3–5 months, and less than six months. Zheng (2000, 2001, 2020): These studies were excluded because they were hospital-based case-control studies. Data was not presented for breastfeeding beyond 12 months. Zhong (2019): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations analyzed were 31 months, with no data on breastfeeding beyond 12 months. Zhou (2007, 2012): These studies were excluded because they did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations used for analysis were less than and greater than six months. Ziegler (2003): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Duration was defined as 12–15 months, which did not meet the inclusion criteria. Zielhuis (1989): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. Breastfeeding durations used in analyses were 0–4 weeks, 2–3 months, 4–7 months, and more than or equal to seven months. Zive (1992): This study was excluded because it did not examine continued breastfeeding. GRADE Working Group grades of evidence were used to assess the quality of studies. High-quality evidence indicates that further research is very unlikely to change confidence in the estimate of effect. Moderate-quality evidence suggests that further research is likely to have an important impact on confidence in the estimate and may change the estimate. Low-quality evidence indicates that further research is very likely to have an important impact on confidence in the estimate and is likely to change the estimate. Very low-quality evidence means there is significant uncertainty about the estimate.
